First we show that if $f(n) = m$, then $\Th{Q} \Proves !A_f(
um n, 
um m)$,
i.e.,  
 egin{align}
  \Th{Q} & \Proves !A_g(
um{m}, 
um{n}, \Obj 0) \land \lforall[w][(w <
    
um{m} \lif \lnot !A_g(w, 
um{n}, \Obj 0))]. 
otag
  \intertext{Since $!A_g(x, z, y)$ represents $g(x, z)$ and $g(m, n) =
    0$ if $f(n) = m$, we have}
\Th{Q} & \Proves !A_g(
um{m}, 
um{n}, \Obj 0). 
otag
\intertext{If $f(n) = m$, then for every $k < m$, $g(k, n) 
eq 0$. So}
\Th{Q} & \Proves \lnot !A_g(
um{k}, 
um{n}, \Obj 0). 
otag
\intertext{We get that}
\Th{Q} & \Proves \lforall[w][(w < 
um{m} \lif \lnot
  !A_g(w, 
um{n}, \Obj 0))]. \ollabel{rep-less}
\end{align}
by \olref{lem:less-zero} in case $m = 0$ and by \olref{lem:less-nsucc} otherwise.

Now let's show that if $f(n) = m$, then $\Th{Q} \Proves
\lforall[y][(!A_f(
um{n}, y) \lif \eq[y][
um{m}])]$.  We again
sketch the argument informally, leaving the formalization to the
reader.

Suppose $!A_f(
um{n}, b)$. From this we get (a) $!A_g(b, 
um{n},
\Obj 0)$ and (b) $\lforall[w][(w < b \lif \lnot !A_g(w, 
um{n}, \Obj
  0))]$.  By \olref{lem:trichotomy}, $(b < 
um{m} \lor 
um{m} < b)
\lor \eq[b][
um{m}]$. We'll show that both $b < 
um{m}$ and $
um{m}
< b$ leads to a contradiction.

If $
um{m} < b$, then $\lnot !A_g(
um{m}, 
um{n}, \Obj 0)$
from~(b). But $m = f(n)$, so $g(m, n) = 0$, and so $\Th{Q} \Proves
!A_g(
um{m}, 
um{n}, \Obj 0)$ since $!A_g$ represents~$g$. So we
have a contradiction.

Now suppose $b < 
um{m}$. Then since $\Th{Q} \Proves \lforall[w][(w <
  
um{m} \lif \lnot !A_g(w, 
um{n}, \Obj 0))]$ by \olref{rep-less}, we
get $\lnot !A_g(b, 
um{n}, \Obj 0)$. This again contradicts~(a).
